sweep_summary: Khmu (khmu1256) is in the catalog as fixed-strict (final/main-syllable stress, word domain, no lexical stress), deciding source Premsrirat 1987 A Khmu Grammar p.5. Both works with stress in the title are Glottolog false positives: the reference pages for 408084 (Wenk 1987, speech rhythm in music) and 604049 (Carlson & Tyler 2018, English pitch accents and attachment) each state the Khmu language code is a 'computerized assignment from \"just\"'; neither concerns Khmu (Carlson & Tyler confirmed English-only via its open PMC copy).., quote verbatim), Suwilai 1999 MKS 29 ('A word has only one strong stress, which is always on the last syllable'), Cooper & Cooper 2001 MKS (PW = (Sr)+Sm, fully stressed main syllable), Svantesson & Karlsson 2004 TAL (stressed major syllable preceded by unstressed minor syllable), and House et al. 2009 Interspeech (downloaded; phrase-final accent only, silent on word stress). All four first-hand statements confirm the catalog's classification; nothing contradicts or refines it. Unread leads: Svantesson 1983 Kammu phonology and morphology (print only, medium priority), Svantesson & House 2006 Phonology and Karlsson et al. 2012 Phonetica (tone/intonation, paywalled, low priority).

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (final stress, final) and as Premsrirat 1987/1999: one strong stress on the last (major) syllable. Adds detail: a three-way strong/weak/unstress grading of syllables (weak stress on minor syllables), a register (two registers, pitch conditioned by the coda) riding on every stressed syllable, and the observation that words are at most two syllables (one UUS trisyllable) in this Khmu Lue variety, against Premsrirat's 'one, two, or three syllables'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable, one strong stress per phonological word ('stress group'), always on the last syllable, which is the major syllable; a preceding minor syllable carries weak stress and a preceding presyllable is unstressed. Words are one or two syllables; the single trisyllable found is unstress-unstress-strong. Every stressed syllable also carries one of two registers (high clear vs low breathy), each realised as two pitches conditioned by the final consonant (§5.11.1, pp.85-99).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three grades: strong stress (major syllable), weak stress (minor syllable, structure WS, e.g. [ˌtamˈpaʔ] 'snapping turtle'), unstress (presyllable, structure US, e.g. [saˈliː] 'corn'). Weak stress is a lesser prominence on the first syllable of a two-syllable word, not a separate rhythmic stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; stress is 'treated as predictable'. Only one trisyllabic word was found (UUS).
new_statements.identity_note: Ong-Arj 1988 describes Khmu Lue of Sob-Phang village, Chiang Klang district, Nan province (a register-contrast Western Khmu variety per Premsrirat 2001 p.128). Wongnoppharalert 1993 describes the Nam Sod village dialect, Tambon Lae, Amphoe Thung Chang, Nan province, which she analyses as having two lexical tones. Premsrirat 2001 surveys seven Khmu dialects across Thailand, Laos, Vietnam and China, splitting them into Eastern (no tone, no register) and Western (register or tone) Khmu; it makes no stress statement for any of them. The catalog's Khmu entry (glottocode khmu1256) covers the language as a whole; all stress statements found so far come from Nan/Chiengrai (Western) varieties.

tone_statements.citation: Karlsson, Anastasia. 2018. Coordination between lexical tones and melody in traditional Kammu singing [カムー語の伝統的歌唱における声調とメロディーの関係]. Onsei Kenkyu (Journal of the Phonetic Society of Japan) 22(3): 30-41.
tone_statements.quote: The cultural setting under study is Kammu, an Austroasiatic language spoken mainly in Laos. Kammu is a tone language where each syllable has a tone, either High or Low. The overarching melodic template is separated from tones to detect if or how lexical tones interact with melody.

tone_statements.citation: Karlsson, Anastasia, Håkan Lundström & Jan-Olof Svantesson. 2014. Preservation of lexical tones in singing in a tone language. Proceedings of Interspeech 2014, Singapore, 1357-1360.
tone_statements.quote: The main question in this investigation is whether a language (in our case the Mon-Khmer language Kammu) with a simple two-tone system uses similar strategies for preserving lexical tones in singing and speech. We investigate the realization of lexical tones in a singing genre which can be described as recitation based on a partly predefined, though still flexible, melodic template. The contrast between High and Low tone is preserved, and is realized mainly at the beginning of the vowel.

tone_statements.citation: Karlsson, Anastasia, David House, Jan-Olof Svantesson & Damrong Tayanin. 2010. Influence of lexical tones on intonation in Kammu. In: Proceedings of Interspeech 2010, 1740-1743.
tone_statements.quote: The aim of this study is to investigate how the presence of lexical tones influences the realization of focal accent and sentence intonation. The language studied is Kammu, a language particularly well suited for the study as it has both tonal and non-tonal dialects. The main finding is that lexical tone exerts an influence on both sentence and focal accent in the tonal dialect to such a strong degree that we can postulate a hierarchy where lexical tone is strongest followed by sentence accent, with focal accent exerting the weakest influence on the F0 contour.

tone_statements.citation: House, David, Anastasia Karlsson, Jan-Olof Svantesson and Damrong Tayanin (2009). The Phrase-Final Accent in Kammu: Effects of Tone, Focus and Engagement. Proc. Interspeech 2009.
tone_statements.quote: Kammu, a Mon-Khmer language spoken primarily in northern Laos by approximately 600,000 speakers, but also in Thailand, Vietnam and China, is a language that has developed lexical tones rather recently, from the point of view of language history. Tones arose in connection with loss of the contrast between voiced and voiceless initial consonants in a number of dialects [6]. One of the main dialects of this language is a tone language with high or low tone on each syllable, while the other main dialect lacks lexical tones. The dialects differ only marginally in other respects.

tone_statements.citation: Svantesson, Jan-Olof & Anastasia Mukhanova Karlsson 2004. Minor syllable tones in Kammu. Proc. International Symposium on Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL 2004), Beijing. ISCA Archive.
tone_statements.quote: This article deals with the Yùan dialect spoken in Nam Tha province in Laos, in the northern part of the Kammu area. Northern Kammu is a tone language with two tones, high and low. Other dialects spoken to the east and south of the the Yùan area are non-tonal. ... The existence of tones in Northern Kammu is a fairly recent innovation. The high and low tones have developed from an earlier contrast between syllable initial voiceless and voiced consonants [10, 12]. For example, Northern Kammu kláa 'eagle' (with high tone) corresponds to Eastern Kammu klaa, while klàa 'stone' (low tone) corresponds to Eastern Kammu glaa.

[...] A main syllable is the syllable that occurs alone as a monosyllabic word or as the last syllable of a disyllabic or trisyllabic word. It is always stressed. Its vowel has full quality. The presyllable, the syllable that comes before the main syllable, is always unstressed and very weak.

Other dialects spoken to the east and south of the the Yùan area are non-tonal. ... The existence of tones in Northern Kammu is a fairly recent innovation. The high and low tones have developed from an earlier contrast between syllable initial voiceless and voiced consonants [10, 12]. For example, Northern Kammu kláa 'eagle' (with high tone) corresponds to Eastern Kammu klaa, while klàa 'stone' (low tone) corresponds to Eastern Kammu glaa.

tone.says: Northern (Yùan) Kammu has two tones, high and low, developed from the old voiced/voiceless onset contrast; the paper documents an additional high vs low tone contrast on unstressed minor syllables (ten minimal pairs, e.g. km.nòh 'cutting-board' vs km.nòh 'weeding period'), confirmed acoustically (~20 Hz F0 difference, p<0.001), and relates it to morphology and tonogenesis.

sources.quote: The main question in this investigation is whether a language (in our case the Mon-Khmer language Kammu) with a simple two-tone system uses similar strategies for preserving lexical tones in singing and speech. We investigate the realization of lexical tones in a singing genre which can be described as recitation based on a partly predefined, though still flexible, melodic template. The contrast between High and Low tone is preserved, and is realized mainly at the beginning of the vowel.
sources.note: Kammu has 'a simple two-tone system'; in recitation-style singing 'the contrast between High and Low tone is preserved, and is realized mainly at the beginning of the vowel', reduplicated syllables ignoring lexical tone.

sources.citation: Karlsson, Anastasia, David House, Jan-Olof Svantesson & Damrong Tayanin. 2010. Influence of lexical tones on intonation in Kammu. In: Proceedings of Interspeech 2010, 1740-1743.
sources.quote: The aim of this study is to investigate how the presence of lexical tones influences the realization of focal accent and sentence intonation. The language studied is Kammu, a language particularly well suited for the study as it has both tonal and non-tonal dialects. The main finding is that lexical tone exerts an influence on both sentence and focal accent in the tonal dialect to such a strong degree that we can postulate a hierarchy where lexical tone is strongest followed by sentence accent, with focal accent exerting the weakest influence on the F0 contour.
sources.note: In the tonal dialect lexical tone dominates the F0 contour - hierarchy lexical tone > sentence accent > focal accent - established by comparison with the non-tonal dialect.
